lede: The objections that come up most often, answered without hedging.

items.q: More carriers means more admin and less volume discount, doesn't it?
items.a: More admin, yes — if it stays manual. That is exactly what the tool absorbs: once the rate sheets are imported, checking three carriers or fifteen takes the same single action. On volume, the effect is real but usually overstated: a discount granted once a year to an incumbent holds up poorly against permanent competition, shipment by shipment. And nothing forces you to fragment everything: many shippers keep two main partners on their regular flows and open the rest to arbitration.

items.q: Which rate sheet formats are accepted?
items.a:
Excel, today: .xls and .xlsx. Rate sheets received as PDFs or scans are not processed yet — we would rather say so than let you find out.

The Excel file does not have to be tidy, though. Merged cells, several tables on one sheet, a column covering two carriers, prices carrying a comment, one tab per departure site, ancillary terms slipped in under the prices: that is what we see every day, and that is what the loading agent is built to read. It shows you on screen what it has understood and asks you to decide wherever two readings are possible.

The structure itself is kept as it is: town-by-carrier matrix, scale by pallet count, flat rate per trip, weight brackets by département. We impose no house format.

You enter your contract formula: fuel share, reference index, base index, revision frequency. The formula stays yours — CarrierBridge imposes none. The tool then recalculates the expected surcharge for each period from published indices and compares it with the rate applied on your invoices. It flags calculation gaps; it does not read your contract and is no substitute for contractual analysis. A flagged gap is a point to raise with your carrier, not a conclusion.

No, and CarrierBridge does not replace one: they answer different questions. A TMS executes — it plans, produces documents, tracks shipments. CarrierBridge arbitrates — it decides who gets the order and at what price, then checks what is invoiced. If you have no TMS, CarrierBridge works on its own. If you have one, the two sit side by side, and a connector can pull your transport orders in automatically.

Your rate sheets, volumes and negotiated prices are yours. They are not shared with other clients, not passed to carriers, and not aggregated into a market index. Data is hosted in Europe, encrypted in transit and at rest, and processed in line with the GDPR. Processing purposes, retention periods and your rights are set out in our privacy policy.

items.q: How long does it take to get started?
items.a: Signing up asks for two fields and no configuration. Expect under ten minutes between creating the account and your first comparison on your own rate sheets: you upload one or two files, enter a typical shipment, and get the ranking. Loading a full register of ten to fifteen carriers then happens as you go, sheet by sheet. Kick-off onboarding lets you move it all across in one go.

Yes, in the Pro and Business plans, at no extra charge. It is in beta: it suggests carriers to approach, it does not qualify them for you and does not replace your tender. CarrierBridge works perfectly well without it — most of the value comes from the rate sheets you already have.

No. CarrierBridge is for shippers only: manufacturers, distributors and traders. The tool exists to compare transport offers, not to issue them. Carriers have no access to the platform and so see neither your rate sheets nor those of their competitors.

items.q: What size of company is CarrierBridge for?
items.a: Shippers with an annual transport spend between €100,000 and €3 million: too small to justify a TMS or a dedicated transport buyer, too large to keep running on spreadsheets. In these companies transport is often handled part-time by an order-management or logistics lead who is not a procurement specialist. The tool is built for exactly that: no configuration expected, a usable result in the first session.
